newsitem.title: INDIA: Forensic experts examine India train bomb wreckage.
newsitem.headline: Forensic experts examine India train bomb wreckage.

text.p: Forensic experts on Wednesday sifted through the wreckage of an Indian train torn apart by a powerful bomb blast, in which 33 people were killed and 66 injured, police officials said.
The explosion occurred on Tuesday when the crowded train was passing through Punjab, the northern state rocked by a bloody conflict with Sikh separatists in the 1980s.
Police officials in Punjab's Bhatinda town said no group had claimed responsibility for the explosion, which ripped through the train as it pulled in to a station in Lehrakhanna town.
"We have experts examining the wreckage," a Bhatinda police spokesman told Reuters by telephone. "We have no knowledge so far about which explosives were used or who was behind this."
Bhatinda is about 25 km (15 miles) from Lehrakhanna. Doctors at Bhatinda's Civil Hospital, where many victims were being treated, said they did not expect the toll to rise further.
State-run Doordarshan television quoted Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral as saying the blast was "an act of desperation by elements opposed to peace and normalcy in the state".
The spokesman said Punjab chief minister Prakash Singh Badal was due to visit the site of the explosion later on Wednesday.
Another Punjab chief minister, Beant Singh, was killed in August 1995 by a suspected Sikh suicide bomber. Prime Minister Indira Gandhi was assassinated by her Sikh bodyguards in 1984.

At least seven people were killed in March in a bomb blast near a busy railway station in Jalandhar, another city in Punjab. Police officials said they suspected Moslem separatists based in the Himalayan state of Jammu and Kashmir had carried out that bombing.
Newspapers quoted local officials as saying Kashmiri rebels might have carried out Tuesday's bombing as well.
The Indian Express newspaper quoted police chief P.C. Dogra as saying a time-bomb made of plastic explosives was probably planted on the train.

Agriculture-rich Punjab shares a border with India's long-time foe Pakistan, which New Delhi accuses of arming and training insurgents. Islamabad denies the charges, saying it provides only diplomatic and moral support to Kashmiri rebels.

More than 20,000 people have died in Punjab since 1984, when discontent with New Delhi turned into an armed insurrection after Gandhi sent troops into the Golden Temple, the Sikhs' holiest shrine, to flush out armed militants holed up there.

Sikh militants fighting for an independent homeland have often targeted trains and buses. The bombing in March was the first major incident of violence since Badal's pro-Sikh Akali Dal state government took power in February.
